about: Cron Planner shows you when a five-field cron expression will actually run. You type or build an expression, choose an IANA timezone, and the tool lists the next 20 execution times, marks the matching days on a monthly calendar, and can look for exact-minute overlaps between two or three schedules. It answers the questions that cause real incidents: does this fire on the days I think it does, what happens on the night the clocks change, and will these two jobs start in the same minute?

The syntax is the classic Vixie-style cron used by crontab on Linux and most hosted schedulers: minute, hour, day of month, month and day of week. It is deliberately strict. There is no seconds field, no Quartz extensions such as `L`, `W` or `?`, no year field, no `@daily` macros and no command to run. If your platform's scheduler uses a different dialect, such as Quartz or a cloud service with six fields, treat the results as a check on the five-field core only.

Predictions are computed in your browser with the standard `Intl.DateTimeFormat` timezone database. The README states there is no runtime network, file access, storage or analytics, so schedule expressions stay on your machine. Clipboard access goes through the host's permission prompt.

Once you know when jobs will fire, [Time Wizard](/time-wizard/) helps convert those instants between zones and epoch formats, and [ID Generator](/id-generator/) can mint identifiers for the jobs themselves.

features.title: Strict five-field parser
features.body: Accepts `*`, lists with commas, ranges with a dash, steps with a slash, month names JAN to DEC and weekday names SUN to SAT. Errors name the field and the problem, such as a descending range or a step of zero.

features.title: Next 20 runs in any IANA timezone
features.body: Run times are generated in the selected zone and shown as real instants, so daylight saving changes are taken into account instead of being approximated with a fixed offset.

features.title: Monthly calendar
features.body: Navigate month by month to see which calendar days contain at least one run. Useful for rules like day 31, Fridays combined with a day of month, or February behaviour.

features.title: Presets as a starting point
features.body: Six presets cover every minute, every five minutes, hourly, daily at 09:00, weekdays at 09:00 and the first of the month at 09:00. Click one, then edit the fields.

features.title: Schedule overlap finder
features.body: Compare two or three expressions and list the exact minutes where all of them fire together. Useful for spotting backup, report and cleanup jobs that would collide.

features.title: Bounded and honest
features.body: Searches look at most 2,196 days ahead (366 times six) and compare at most 5,000 candidate runs. When the overlap search stops at its cap the result is marked as truncated, and an empty result is not proof the schedules never meet.

blocks.text: Steps count from the beginning of the range, not from the current time. `*/7` in the minute field gives 0, 7, 14, 21, 28, 35, 42, 49 and 56, and then it restarts at 0 in the next hour, so the gap between 56 and 0 is only four minutes. That is a frequent source of uneven schedules.

sections.heading: Day of month and day of week combine with OR

blocks.text: When both the day-of-month and day-of-week fields are restricted, a day matches if it satisfies either one. So `0 9 1 * 1` runs at 09:00 on the first of every month and also every Monday, not only on Mondays that fall on the first. If one of the two fields is exactly `*`, only the other applies. This matches the behaviour documented for Vixie cron.
To run only when both conditions hold, schedule on the more specific one and test the other inside the job, for example run daily and have the script exit unless the date is a Monday.

A cron time like 02:30 is a wall-clock time, and in zones with daylight saving it can exist zero, one or two times on a given day. When clocks spring forward, the skipped wall time does not exist and the planner omits that run. When clocks fall back, a repeated wall time can appear as two distinct instants, so you may see two runs one hour apart.

Real cron daemons differ here. Some run a job that falls in the gap shortly after the jump, and some treat the fall-back hour specially for wildcard jobs. The planner shows what the clock arithmetic says, not what your particular daemon does. Servers set to UTC avoid the ambiguity entirely, which is why many teams schedule in UTC and convert for display.

example.title: Work out whether a backup and a report collide

blocks.text: Two jobs share a database. The backup is `0 */6 * * *` (every six hours on the hour) and the report is `0 6 * * 1-5` (06:00 on weekdays). Set the timezone to `UTC`, open the overlap finder and enter both expressions.

items: Check each expression alone first. The backup shows 00:00, 06:00, 12:00 and 18:00 every day. The report shows 06:00 Monday to Friday.
Run the comparison. The overlaps are every weekday at 06:00, because that is the only minute both fire.
Change the backup to `30 */6 * * *` and compare again. The overlap list is empty, because the backup now fires at half past the hour.
Remember that an empty list is bounded by the search window, but here both schedules repeat daily, so the empty result is reliable.

blocks.text: Result: you move the backup by 30 minutes rather than relying on the jobs to take turns. For a job running in `America/New_York` instead of UTC, repeat with that zone selected and check the week of a clock change, when a 02:30 job will vanish on spring-forward night.

limits: Five fields only. Quartz expressions with seconds, `L`, `W`, `#` or `?`, `@reboot` style macros and six-field cloud scheduler formats are rejected.
This is a planner, not an execution verifier. It cannot know about missed runs, overlapping executions, daemon downtime or per-platform jitter.
Predictions beyond the next 2,196 days are not generated, which matters for very rare schedules such as `0 0 29 2 *` that fire only in leap years.
For unusual historical timezone transitions, results depend on the timezone data shipped with your browser.
Overlap search inspects at most 5,000 candidates. Treat a truncated or empty result as inconclusive.

faq.question: Why does my job run on days I did not expect?
faq.answer: If both day-of-month and day-of-week are restricted, cron matches either. `0 9 1 * 1` runs on the first of the month and on every Monday. Leave one of them as `*` to avoid this.

faq.question: Is Sunday 0 or 7?
faq.answer: Both are accepted and mean Sunday. Names such as SUN also work, as do ranges like `MON-FRI`.

faq.question: Why is `*/45` not every 45 minutes?
faq.answer: Steps count from the start of the range, so the minute field yields 0 and 45 in each hour. The next run after :45 is :00, only 15 minutes later.

faq.question: Does the tool support seconds or Quartz syntax?
faq.answer: No. Only the five standard fields are supported. Expressions with extra fields, `?`, `L` or `W` are reported as errors.

faq.question: Are my expressions sent anywhere?
faq.answer: No. The planner computes everything in the page and makes no network requests. Copy buttons use the clipboard only when you press them.
